message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In fact, the estimate most often quoted is the **Shannon number**, which is roughly

\[
N_{\text{positions}} \;\approx\; 10^{43}\text{–}10^{44}
\]

This figure counts *legal* positions – i.e., arrangements that could actually occur in a real game following all the rules (including checks, castling rights, en‑passant possibilities, etc.).  

If you include *illegal* arrangements (e.g., two kings in check, too many pawns on a file, etc.), the count rises to about

\[
N_{\text{all}} \;\approx\; 10^{47}\text{–}10^{48}.
\]

So, in short, there are on the order of **tens of trillions of trillions of trillions** of possible chess positions.  (For comparison, the number of atoms in the observable universe is about \(10^{80}\), so the chess position space is still far smaller than that, but still far beyond human enumeration.)
